units.student_markdown:
### Some people believe that secondary schools should require students to take part in community projects. Others think participation should be voluntary. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Community projects can connect school learning with the needs of other people. Some argues that every secondary student should participate, while others prefer voluntary involvement. I believe schools should provide a short shared introduction, but students should be able to choose whether to continue and which activity to join.

A common programme gives teenagers opportunities that they might not finds alone. For example, a class could help a local library organise a reading event. Students would have to divide tasks, speak to staff and explain information clearly to visitors. These responsibilities make communication more concrete than a classroom discussion. One successful event proves that compulsory projects make every teenager responsible. Schools can also provide transport and equipments, so participation is less dependent on what a family can afford. This matters because an opportunity should not be available only to students who already have useful contacts outside school.

Nevertheless, making a large commitment compulsory can reduce the value of the activity. Some students have responsibilities in home, and a fixed schedule may prevent them from taking part comfortably. Others may attend only to satisfy a rule rather than pay attention to the people they are helping. A voluntary programme allows them to select work that fits their interests. Schools should give students enough informations about different options, and project leaders should explain what each role involves. If students will choose a suitable role, they are more likely to remain involved beyond a single session.

In conclusion, both access and personal choice deserve consideration. A brief introductory experience can give all students a chance to learn what community work involves, while voluntary continuation respects different circumstances. Schools should judge the programme by the quality of participation and feedback from the community, rather than attendance alone.

### Порядок работы

Сначала запиши свои языковые правки и объясни проблему одного аргумента. После разбора создай отдельную версию, затем проверь себя на другом эссе. Исправлять каждое предложение не нужно. Только вымышленные учебные тексты; автоматического band нет.

### Первый текст

Some people believe that secondary schools should require students to take part in community projects. Others think participation should be voluntary. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

G2: opportunities that they might not finds alone → opportunities that they might not find alone. После might нужна базовая форма глагола. Альтернативы: opportunities that may be difficult to find alone

G3: provide transport and equipments → provide transport and equipment. Equipment в значении оборудования неисчисляемое; для нескольких предметов можно использовать pieces of equipment. Альтернативы: provide transport and the necessary pieces of equipment

G4: have responsibilities in home → have responsibilities at home. Устойчивая предложная группа at home. Альтернативы: have duties to fulfil at home

G5: enough informations about different options → enough information about different options. Information в этом значении неисчисляемое. Альтернативы: sufficient information about different options

G6: If students will choose a suitable role → If students choose a suitable role. Обычное реальное будущее условие: present simple в if-clause. Это не универсальный запрет will во всех if-clause. Альтернативы: If students chose a suitable role, they might remain involved for longer.

Историю события нужно связать с ответственностью конкретного участника, а не скачком перейти к универсальному доказательству. Это авторское направление ручного разбора, не калиброванная оценка критерия.

This matters because an opportunity should not be available only to students who already have useful contacts outside school.

### Новый текст

Some people think that employers should allow staff to choose their working hours. Others believe fixed hours are necessary. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

G1: The hours people works → The hours people work. People — множественное подлежащее относительного предложения. Альтернативы: People’s working hours

G2: it easier for employees managing → it easier for employees to manage. Конструкция make it easier for someone to do something. Альтернативы: it easier for employees to handle

G3: These arrangements may helps → These arrangements may help. После may используется базовая форма. Альтернативы: These arrangements can help

G4: agree an clear deadline → agree a clear deadline. Clear начинается с согласного звука. Альтернативы: agree on a clear deadline

G5: A small reception team cannot all chooses → A small reception team cannot all choose. После cannot нужна базовая форма. Альтернативы: The members of a small reception team cannot all choose

G6: an unreasonable burden to colleagues → an unreasonable burden for colleagues. Редакция для ясности: a burden on/for colleagues. Burden to someone возможно в соответствующей конструкции; исходную фразу не считать универсально неграмматичной. Альтернативы: an unreasonable burden on colleagues

Аргумент: My neighbour works flexible hours and enjoys the job, so every employer would become more productive by removing fixed schedules.

Удовлетворённость одного работника не устанавливает производительность всех работодателей. Объясни конкретную пользу гибкости и условие, при котором она возможна.

Вариант развития: Avoiding a difficult journey may leave this employee better able to focus on an independent task. However, that benefit depends on meeting deadlines and maintaining necessary contact; it does not establish that every workplace should abandon fixed hours.

Task Response: Обе позиции рассмотрены; автор допускает гибкость для самостоятельных задач и общее время для зависимых услуг. Счастливый сосед не доказывает производительность каждого работодателя. Это авторское направление ручного разбора, не калиброванная оценка критерия.

Coherence and Cohesion: Польза для личного расписания сопоставлена с необходимостью совместной доступности. Пример про приёмную объясняет исключение из общей гибкости; вывод сохраняет условную позицию. Это авторское направление ручного разбора, не калиброванная оценка критерия.

Lexical Resource: Productive описывает результативность, enjoys — отношение работника: это разные утверждения. Burden on/for colleagues допустимы в соответствующем контексте; редкое слово не обязательно точнее. Это авторское направление ручного разбора, не калиброванная оценка критерия.

Grammatical Range and Accuracy: Проверь people work, to manage после easier и базовые формы после may/cannot. В a clear deadline артикль зависит от начального звука. Это авторское направление ручного разбора, не калиброванная оценка критерия.

Пример новой версии, не единственно правильный:

The hours people work affect both their personal routines and the service an organisation provides. Some favour allowing staff to choose their schedules, whereas others support fixed hours for everyone. In my view, flexibility is useful when tasks can be completed independently, but shared availability is necessary when colleagues or customers depend on an immediate response.

Flexible hours can make it easier for employees to manage ordinary responsibilities. A person who travels a long distance could begin earlier and avoid the busiest period on public transport. Someone with an appointment could adjust the start of the day without abandoning the whole working day. These arrangements may help workers concentrate when they are available. Avoiding a difficult journey may leave this employee better able to focus on an independent task. However, that benefit depends on meeting deadlines and maintaining necessary contact; it does not establish that every workplace should abandon fixed hours. An organisation can ask staff to agree a clear deadline and explain how they will communicate. This keeps flexibility connected to completing useful work rather than simply spending less time in the workplace.

However, some services require people to be present together. A small reception team cannot all choose to work at times when the building is closed to visitors. Similarly, a team solving an urgent technical problem needs to know when other members can be reached. Fixed hours make this coordination easier, although identical schedules may be unnecessary for every task. Employers should identify the periods when shared coverage matters and let staff make choices around them. Clear expectations can prevent an arrangement that helps one person from creating an unreasonable burden for colleagues.

In conclusion, neither complete freedom nor one rigid timetable suits all work. Employers should consider the demands of the service, agree shared periods where necessary and review the arrangement with employees. This approach gives personal choice a place without assuming that flexibility automatically improves every organisation.

Regular reading can be difficult even for people who would like to do more of it. A person may have access to books but still struggle to make reading part of an ordinary week. Two obstacles are setting an unrealistic goal and choosing material that does not fit the reader's interests or available attention. Small adjustments can make the habit more manageable.

An ambitious plan can turn reading into a source of pressure. Someone who expects to finish a long book every week may feel discouraged after a busy day. Missing one session can then seem like a reason to abandon the whole plan. A smaller target may reduce the pressure to finish a fixed number of books and make it easier to return after a missed session. However, the person still needs a suitable opportunity to read, so the target should remain flexible rather than become another universal rule. A more realistic approach is to choose a small period that fits the person's routine and allow the plan to change. Reading a few pages while waiting for transport may be feasible on some days, while another day may offer no suitable opportunity. The purpose is to create a repeatable practice rather than meet a rigid public target.

Another obstacle is selecting a book only because it is famous or considered impressive. If its language or subject is unsuitable, the reader may spend more time struggling to continue than engaging with the ideas. People could try a short sample before committing to a whole book and ask for recommendations based on their interests. Libraries can make this easier by offering different formats and clear information about collections. Readers should also feel able to change books without treating that decision as failure. Discovering an unsuitable text provides information that can guide the next choice.

In conclusion, unrealistic expectations and unsuitable material can both interrupt a reading habit. Flexible goals and informed choices may reduce these obstacles. They cannot create extra time in every situation, but they can help readers build a practice that responds to their own circumstances rather than an idealised schedule.
